title: Randa Ayoubi's 1994 Pitch in Amman: Ideas With No Land to Pledge
dek: In 1994 Randa Ayoubi tried to raise money in Jordan for a digital-content company when investors wanted land or factories as collateral.

story.event: Starting a digital education and animation company in Amman without collateral
story.summary: In 1994 Randa Ayoubi started what became Rubicon in Amman with about $140,000 of investment, after investors who wanted land or factory assets as collateral dismissed her plan for technology-based educational content, beginning with CD-ROMs for village children, as madness. The company moved into animation, pitched Ben & Izzy to Cartoon Network in 2006, sold a 30 per cent stake to GrowthGate Capital in 2009 and by 2011 had offices in Amman, Los Angeles, Manila and Dubai.
paragraphs: In 1994, in Amman, Randa Ayoubi went looking for backing for an idea that, by her later account, most of the businesspeople she approached called madness. Her first business model was a minibus that would carry educational CD-ROMs, which she produced, to children in small villages, where a later profile said Jordan's educational gaps were widest. She said she was surprised by how firmly it was rejected: some investors would not even sit down and listen.

The difficulty, as she described it in 2011, was partly the technology, which was unfamiliar in the region, and partly the kind of venture she was asking people to fund: "something that was not a farm, a factory. It's ideas." Investors asked what she could guarantee as collateral, land or assets of some kind, and she had nothing to offer. Most people, she said, gave her the time of day at first only "to get me off their backs."

She started anyway, with about $140,000 of investment; the company's own history calls it a small venture capital project. She held to one stance from the beginning: "Even when we started and we were very small and didn't have any money, we always thought of ourselves as a global company." The work moved from educational content towards animation. In 2006 Rubicon pitched an animated series, Ben & Izzy, about an American boy and his Jordanian friend, to Cartoon Network; The New York Times called it perhaps the most memorable pitch stunt among nearly 300 proposals the network received each year.

In 2009, fifteen years after she started, the Bahrain-based private equity fund GrowthGate Capital bought 30 per cent of Rubicon, by then described as the Middle East's largest animation workshop and working with MGM on a Pink Panther series. In 2011 Ernst & Young named Ayoubi Jordan's Entrepreneur of the Year; the company had offices in Amman, Los Angeles, Manila and Dubai. Asked that year what had changed investors' minds, she pointed to her country, which, she noted, has no natural resources: "Investors would never say no to something that helped young Jordanians better themselves."

quote.text: This speculative genius is the madness of few for the gain of the world. The projectors are sacrificed, but the public is the gainer.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Ayoubi's investors used the same word Emerson does: madness. Emerson credits such people with much of what the public later enjoys, but adds, without comfort, that the projectors are often sacrificed. Her story is one of being proved right; his line is a reminder that belief alone does not decide who is.

reflection: Ayoubi was asking people to back something they could not walk around or pledge against a loan. The investors who wanted land were not foolish; they were using the only measure they trusted. What changed their minds, in her telling, was not one argument but years of visible work and a purpose they already cared about.

Emerson keeps the story honest. Many people told their idea is madness are never proved right, and some pay heavily for trying. If your own work is hard to explain to a banker, it may help to say plainly what you are risking, and what you are not prepared to lose.
invitation: Write one sentence describing what you are building for someone who only trusts farms and factories. Use words a sceptical relative would accept, then leave it there for today.

cross_checks.claim: Ayoubi started the company in Amman in 1994 with about $140,000 of investment
Her first work was educational CD-ROMs for children in Jordanian villages
Investors dismissed the idea as madness and wanted collateral she did not have
GrowthGate Capital took a 30 per cent stake in Rubicon in 2009
By 2011-2013 Rubicon had offices in Amman, Los Angeles, Manila and Dubai

research_notes: The founding episode rests mainly on Ayoubi's own account in two 2011 interviews by the same journalist, Farah Halime, for The National and Institutional Investor; they agree on the 1994 start, the $140,000, the CD-ROM idea, the 'madness' reaction and the lack of collateral, but they are not fully independent of each other, so the story attributes these points to her ('by her later account', 'she said'). Neither says who supplied the $140,000; the company's archived history calls it 'a small venture capital project'. Funding is therefore marked 'unknown' rather than the slate's 'bootstrapped'. Whether the minibus scheme ever ran is not stated; the story calls it her 'first business model', as The National does. Wikipedia names the predecessor company Jordan Training Technology Group (1994-2004) and says it began by training bankers in multimedia skills, but no loadable source confirmed this, so the story does not use the name or the banker training, and says only that the work 'moved from educational content towards animation'. The New York Times 'pitch stunt' description is taken from The National's quotation because the Times article is blocked. In 2009 Rubicon also said it expected more than $100m in revenue the following year; that is a company projection and is not used. The Red Sea Astrarium resort in Aqaba ($1.5 billion announced in 2011) is left out because its later fate could not be established from loadable sources; the story ends with dated facts from 2009-2013 and makes no claim about the company today. The Emerson passage is from his essay on speculative builders of railways, mills and mines; it is applied by analogy, and its word 'madness' echoes Ayoubi's account. The company field reads "Rubicon (later Rubicon Group)" rather than the full name Rubicon Group Holding because the repeat screen flagged (but passed) an unrelated edition on Vehbi Koç, apparently over the shared word "Holding"; it is a different person and company.
